street_smart.title: Your neighbours are in the middle of a loud, escalating family argument — raised voices, one of them has grabbed a kitchen knife off the counter. You've known them for years and want to help calm things down. What's the smartest move?
street_smart.based_on: The Times of India, Sept 7 — a man was assaulted with a machete after stepping in to mediate a family dispute in Bengaluru. This mediator-gets-attacked mechanism hasn't been used as a street-smart scenario in the last three weeks.
street_smart.situation: You're standing at their door. One of them notices you and says, 'Stay out of it, this is between us' — but the shouting hasn't stopped.

choices.text: Step back from the doorway, call the police (112) or a domestic-violence helpline from a safe distance, and let trained responders de-escalate the situation.
choices.feedback: Correct. Once a weapon is already out, a dispute has crossed from 'argument' to 'active risk' — mediators are seen as taking a side, and anger already running hot can redirect onto you in seconds. Police and trained responders are equipped to de-escalate; you calling them fast is the highest-leverage thing you can do.

choices.text: Walk in and physically position yourself between them, reasoning that your long friendship with the family gives you the standing to calm things down.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. Familiarity feels like protection, but it isn't — in the exact incident this scenario is based on, the person attacked was mediating a dispute, not a stranger to it. Once anger and a weapon are both in the room, being 'between' the two people means being in the path of whichever way the aggression turns.

choices.text: Shout at them to stop from the doorway without stepping fully inside, hoping the noise and your presence alone will break the tension.
choices.feedback: Risky. Shouting into an already-heated argument can escalate it further rather than calming it, and you're still close enough to be pulled in or struck if the person holding the knife reacts suddenly.

choices.text: Quietly close your own door and do nothing, assuming it's a private family matter that will resolve on its own.
choices.feedback: Risky. A weapon has already come out — this has moved past 'private matter' into a safety situation. Doing nothing risks someone getting seriously hurt when a quick, safe call to the police could have brought help in time.

takeaways: Once a weapon appears in a dispute, don't physically position yourself between the people involved — call 112 or a local domestic-violence helpline from a safe distance instead.
Being familiar with the people involved doesn't protect you; in-the-moment anger doesn't reliably distinguish 'mediator' from 'target.'
If you must communicate, do it by phone or through a locked door rather than standing in the doorway or entering the room.
